title: Jack Purvis and the drive to California
summary: Back in Shreveport he brought Jack Purvis, who abruptly left for California and fled El Paso over past gun smuggling; Barnet later spotted him in Les Heidt's band in disguise.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: But the second time we went to Shreveport, to the hotel there, I took Jack Purvis and a trumpet player by the name of Harley Booth, and a guitar player by the name

of Scoop Thompson, and we joined Flem's band and we used to play up in the roof garden there in the summertime, and Jack Purvis is a -- I don't know if you've ever heard of him -- he was a fantastic musician, a fantastic trumpet player. He could do everything that Louis Armstrong could do in those days. He had a tremendous range for those days. He had himself a G or an A anytime he wanted it. And well, the Louisiana Symphony came to town, and Jack somehow got himself into a deal there where he was going to play the Carnival of Venice with the symphony, and he was rehearsing with them. That and something else he was going to play. And Jack was pretty crazy. For no reason whatsoever he says, "Come on, let's go to California." And I said, "Well, you've got to do that thing with the symphony." He said, "Oh, the hell with it." So we got in the car and we left, and we got out as far as El Paso, and it seems that Jack had been there before, and he had been smuggling guns across the border in his previous time there, and the people that were in power at the time he was smuggling were now out of power, and we beat a hasty retreat. We got split up. And I went on to the Coast. I didn't see him at all until one night, I walked into the old Cotton Club out in Culver City. I had no idea what had happened to him. And I heard this trumpet, and I looked up at the bandstand, and here's Purvis up there, he's got his face stained and he's playing trumpet with Les Heidt's orchestra.
Now, I said, "What are you doing?" He said, "Sshh, don't tell anybody who I am. They're after me."
I said, "Who's after you?" He said, "The government." I think he was probably right. I didn't believe him at the time, but he did wind up spending his last days in jail.
